newsitem.title: JAPAN: Little reaction to report of assault by US sailor.
newsitem.headline: Little reaction to report of assault by US sailor.

text.p: While an investigation of a possible assault by a U.S. sailor against a Japanese woman comes at a bad time for U.S.-Japan military relations, the incident has not brought much reaction in Japan.

In September 1995, the widely publicised rape of a 12-year old Okinawan schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen triggered public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence on Okinawa in southern Japan and prompted an official review.

The latest case comes as Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto is pushing through new legislation to force private landowners to continue leasing their land for U.S. bases and just before a high-profile visit by U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen.

In the case, a sailor at the U.S. military headquarters at Yokosuka, near Tokyo, is being held on suspicion of sexually assaulting and beating up his Japanese girlfriend in the early hours of Thursday.
"We have not received complaints from citizens over the case, and this incident cannot be compared with the Okinawa (rape) case," a Yokosuka city spokesman said on Friday.
Japanese media also reported the Yokosuka incident as a violent quarrel between a couple, and not a rape or sexual assault, based on Japanese police assessment of the case.
The Yokosuka city spokesman said not even leftist activists, normally at the forefront of anti-base campaigns, have spoken out on the case.
"This looks like a case of domestic violence," he said.
Yokosuka, 40 km (25 miles) south of Tokyo, is the largest U.S. Navy base in Japan and homeport of the aircraft carrier USS Independence.

The woman was in hospital with a broken collar bone. She told investigators that the sailor, whom she said she had been dating for eight months, threw her on a bed after a quarrel. No formal charges had yet been filed.
The U.S. Defence Department said on Thursday it was concerned that the case could harm U.S.-Japan relations at a critical time for U.S. military bases.
In another embarrassment for U.S. forces, police in South Korea on Thursday arrested a U.S. army sergeant on suspicion of smuggling automatic rifles out of a base.
News of the assault case came on the same day Hashimoto asked parliament to revise a law to enable his government to renew leases on land for U.S. military bases.

At stake are plots of land owned by 3,000 anti-bases activists whose leases expire on May 14. Hashimoto needed the revision to temporarily extend leases while an Okinawa land expropriation committee finished a lengthy series of hearings.

On Thursday, Hashimoto won the support of the main opposition party for the revision and parliament looked set to approve it by the end of April when Hashimoto travels to Washington for talks with U.S. President Bill Clinton.
Hashimoto also meets Cohen in Tokyo next week.
